PCR can provide timely results with improved sensitivity over culture. Use careful specimen collection and transport to better ensure that healthcare providers obtain diagnostic test results that reliably inform patient diagnosis. Overview With the rise in reported pertussis cases since the early 1990s, healthcare providers are increasingly likely to see more patients with suspected pertussis. PCR is an important tool for timely diagnosis of pertussis and is increasingly available to healthcare providers. PCR is a molecular technique used to detect DNA sequences of the Bordetella pertussis bacterium. Unlike culture, PCR doesn't require viable (live) bacteria present in the specimen. pages.text: Beverly Goodman studies ancient catastrophes to prevent disasters | National Geographic Beverly Goodman searches underwater to help us survive future emergencies. Photograph by REBECCA HALE, NGM staff Premium MAGAZINE INNOVATOR She studies ancient catastrophes to prevent future disasters This ‘disaster scientist’ is uncovering clues buried underwater that may save lives today. By Nina Strochlic Published April 23, 2020 • 2 min read This story appears in the May 2020 issue of National Geographic magazine. When Beverly Goodman was in elementary school, she gave a series of presentations on her favorite topic: disasters. She told her classmates about the eruption that buried Pompeii , the black plague , and famous shipwrecks like the Titanic and the Lusitania . Today, at 45, she’s a marine geoarchaeologist who excavates coastlines for clues to erosion, past tsunamis , and other disasters. “It’s funny now that I’m a disaster scientist, basically,” she says. “It all came together.” Human settlements have long been built around access to water. Goodman studies how coastal change affected our ancestors: Were people forced to leave? Did they find innovative ways to adapt to the changes? This knowledge, she says, can help us “prepare responsibly for what this landscape is going to look like in the future.” That was the case when Goodman and her team of scientists proved tsunamis had struck the coast of what is now Israel over the course of thousands of years. Globally, around one-third of all food produced for human consumption is lost or wasted each year, contributing an estimated 8–10 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Reducing this waste is central to FAO’s mandate on food security and sustainable agrifood systems and monitoring food waste at FAO HQ helps the organization ‘walk the talk’ in its own operations. Building on previous editions, the Food Waste Initiative used FAO’s canteens and catering areas as key entry points for engagement, pairing real-time food waste monitoring with on-the-spot awareness-raising among participants. The goal was to make every meal an opportunity to rethink consumption and food waste. During the WFF, the CER Team deployed eleven dedicated volunteers across all five Food Waste Stations in FAO canteens , plus an extra station near the food truck area. The first confirmed case involved an eight-month-old girl who developed a high fever on 21 February, followed by a widespread rash. Her parents sought treatment at Maharishi Valmiki Infectious Diseases Hospital, where laboratory testing confirmed measles infection. The hospital promptly notified the District Immunization Office, which started an outbreak investigation. Accredited social health activist (ASHA) workers, frontline health staff and a WHO-supported team visited the area to identify suspected cases. Samples were collected from four children with symptoms of fever and rash – two tested positive for measles, confirming the outbreak. Measles is a highly contagious disease that spreads through an infected person’s coughing, sneezing or breathing. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and rash. pages.text: Bhutan is close to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies Skip to main content WHO/Bhutan Bhutan is close to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies © Credits Bhutan is close to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies 1 September 2026 Highlights Reading time: Rabies used to be a serious public health threat in Bhutan, especially in the southern border districts. Now, the country is on the verge of a major achievement: eliminating dog-mediated human rabies for good. This progress didn't happen overnight. It is the result of strong government leadership, years of sustained surveillance, rapid outbreak response, easy access to rabies vaccines after exposure, mass dog vaccination drives, better dog population management, and strong collaboration between human and animal health sectors. Bhutan has not recorded a single human rabies case since 2023—more than two years running. Having met WHO's requirements, Bhutan put together its official National Dossier on the Elimination of Dog-Mediated Human Rabies and asked WHO to independently validate this achievement in June 2026. From 18–21 August 2026, a team of international experts visited Bhutan to verify Bhutan's claim. They verified surveillance and programme data, carried out field visits, assessed programme implementation efforts, and met with key stakeholders across human and animal health sectors. The team confirmed Bhutan's progress and offered recommendations to help sustain Bhutan's achievements.

What is Big Data? Big data is a term used to describe data sources that are fast-changing, large in both size and breadth of information, and come from sources other than surveys. Examples include retail and payroll transactions, satellite images, and "smart" devices. Big data also includes administrative data from federal, state, and local governments, as well as third party providers. The Hummingbird Springs Wilderness , northeast of this area, is separated from the Big Horn Wilderness by a jeep trail. Nine miles of the jumbled Big Horn Mountains ridgeline cross the wilderness. This wilderness offers many recreation opportunities such as hiking, backpacking, rock climbing, photography and nature study. Rugged ridges challenge expert climbers, while side canyons and plains offer easier hiking. pages.text: Bihar achieves historic first in lymphatic filariasis elimination Skip to main content (©WHO) © Credits Bihar achieves historic first in lymphatic filariasis elimination Fifty-five of Bihar’s 57 implementation units have passed Transmission Assessment Survey-1, showing low lymphatic filariasis transmission. As a result, three districts have stopped Mass Drug Administration, advancing India’s LF elimination goal. 23 June 2026 Reading time: For generations, families across Bihar have lived under the burden of lymphatic filariasis (LF), a preventable neglected tropical disease that can cause lifelong disability, social stigma, and economic hardship. For the first time since launching Mass Drug Administration (MDA) in 2004, Bihar has successfully cleared its first Transmission Assessment Survey (TAS)—the standardized survey used to determine whether LF transmission has fallen below levels required to prevent new infection. Passing TAS allows the national programme to stop MDA and transition to post-MDA surveillance. The achievement is significant not only for Bihar but also for India’s goal of eliminating LF as a public health problem by 2027. As of May 2026, LF is endemic in 350 districts across 20 states and union territories in India. Bihar has faced one of the toughest challenges: all 38 districts and 592 implementation units are endemic for the disease. pages.text: Billions of T. rex likely roamed the Earth, paleontologists report | National Geographic Paleontologists figured out how many T. rex lived on Earth—and they found that about 20,000 would have been alive at any given time during a two- to three-million year timespan. Illustration by STOCKTREK IMAGES, Nat Geo Image Collection SCIENCE NEWS Billions of T. rex likely roamed the Earth, paleontologists report The iconic predator’s estimated abundance means the T. rex fossils we have today are exceedingly rare. By Michael Greshko Published April 19, 2021 • 6 min read If you traveled back in time 67 million years ago to ancient Montana, you’d be entering the realm of a tyrant: the iconic predator Tyrannosaurus rex . Before you venture into that lost world, though, you might want to know: On average, how close is the nearest T. rex to you? That might sound like an impossible thing to know—but after crunching through two decades’ worth of T. rex research, a new study provides estimates of the animal’s population density. In all likelihood, a T. rex would be within 15 miles of you, if not much closer. The new study, published last Thursday in Science , also translates these population densities into estimates for how many T. rex ever lived. On average, researchers estimate that some 20,000 T. rex lived at any one time and that about 127,000 generations of the dinosaurs lived and died. Those averages imply that a total of 2.5 billion T. rex lived in the species’ native North America, possibly as far north as Alaska and as far south as Mexico, over a two- to three-million-year timespan.
